title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR decision rule, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline under a frozen protocol. Execution used a shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM candidate per pair) and model_calls_used = 300 (declared model: gpt-5-mini). Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. No validator-detected forbidden-reachability occurred and no repair calls were invoked; consequently the preregistered hypothesis about repair efficacy was not testable in this run. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. We present a compact technical definition of the scoring predicate and validators, a concise presentation of the principal statistics, artifact-grounded interpretation, and design lessons for follow-up stress tests intended to exercise the repair path. Key artifacts (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, and analysis outputs) are archived and summarized below to permit verification.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operational productivity gains but raises acute operator concerns: generated configurations can unintentionally expand attack surface, violate access-control policies, or disrupt availability. Prior system and survey work therefore recommends constrained generation, execution validators, and generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipelines as mitigations [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. Yet there is little preregistered, deterministic evidence that embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside an LLM-driven GVR loop meaningfully reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations when adversarial intents are present.

We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory experiment (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) to answer one focused research question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier in a GVR loop reduce the incidence of validator-detected forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our contributions are evidence-grounded and artifact-archived: (1) a machine-readable preregistration and deterministic paired N = 300 design; (2) a Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation run using two deterministic validators combined by logical OR and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics to economize model calls; (3) a compact, artifact-verified presentation of the confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300, no repairs invoked) together with a Clopper–Pearson upper bound on an undetected violation rate; and (4) concrete design lessons and reproducibility guidance (budget vs inferential-power trade-offs) to inform stress tests that actually exercise the repair path. We emphasize at the outset that because the verifier never flagged violations, this run provides evidence about verifier insertion under the chosen contract (shared initial candidate) rather than evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations.
sections.related_work:
Three strands of prior work frame this study. First, GVR/verification-loop architectures improve correctness for generated code and IaC by using execution-oracle feedback to drive repair; realized gains depend heavily on verifier fidelity and repair strategy [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W7124141852]. Second, surveys and NetOps systems papers report LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend integrating validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce operational risk [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Third, emulation/testbed work demonstrates that execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation while warning of external-validity gaps when porting results to heterogeneous production devices or live traffic [https://openalex.org/W4406170828].

This work differs by preregistering a deterministic paired test that (a) fixes generation semantics to control model-call budget, (b) archives per-episode validator traces for auditability, and (c) reports how the choice of generation semantics interacts with the ability to test repair efficacy.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: The preregistered confirmatory design fixed N = 300 matched pairs (150 benign seeds each paired with a programmatic adversarial variant), primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, and analysis = exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). Prespecified CIs were bootstrap-percentile; the final analysis used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 (recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Sampling and deduplication rules followed the preregistration (exact duplicates removed; fuzzy duplicates with normalized edit distance < 0.15 excluded). The full preregistration is cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1 (archived).

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To conserve provider usage we preregistered a shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each matched intent pair a single initial LLM candidate is generated and replayed to both arms (baseline receives the shared candidate; guarded validates and may invoke up to one repair call if validators report forbidden reachability). Under this contract model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs (execution manifest records model_calls_used = 300 and stage_counts: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). This contract trades model-call savings for reduced independent-sample variability between arms and therefore reduces the chance of observing discordant violating outputs needed to demonstrate repair efficacy.

Operational predicate and validators (concise technical definition): The scoring predicate used in this study is the validator-detected forbidden-reachability predicate. Operationally, we labeled a configuration as violating when any deterministic validator reported a reachability or policy outcome that newly enabled an access or path that the emulator/validator set considered forbidden under the task's intent constraints. Two deterministic validators were employed: (1) a containerized execution-oriented validator (Batfish-style) that evaluates forwarding state and policy effects in the emulated FRR forwarding plane, and (2) a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer that inspects the induced connectivity graph. We combined these with logical OR: a pair is labeled violating if any validator reports forbidden reachability. Limitations: these validators approximate operational semantics and may not capture all ACL/route-policy semantics, dynamic convergence effects, or ECMP subtleties; per-episode validator outputs and the canonical validator identifier (validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version = '5.0') are archived in execution/scoring/*.json for inspection.

Intervention arms and repair policy: Baseline = replay of shared initial candidate (no repair). Guarded = same shared candidate validated; if a validator reported the forbidden-reachability predicate, the preregistered repair policy allowed up to one repair LLM call using an archived repair prompt template. Across the run no repair was triggered because validators never flagged forbidden reachability (per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied = false in all scoring artifacts).

Execution and determinism: The environment used Dockerized FRRouting-style device images and deterministic orchestration; per-task seeds, task payloads, and emulator composition are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl. Provider-call accounting and execution manifest records (start/completion timestamps, completed episode count = 600, failed = 0) are included in the evidence bundle.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed = 600; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300 under the shared_initial_candidate contract (execution manifest). Primary confirmatory counts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Derived statistics: baseline_success_rate = 300/300 = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 300/300 = 1.0; paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI of the paired risk-difference (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). Because no violations were observed, the repair policy was never invoked (per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied = false in execution/scoring/*.json).

Descriptive bound on undetected baseline violations: Observing 0/300 validator-detected violations produces a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%). This bound quantifies the maximum baseline violation rate compatible with the observed zero-event outcome under standard binomial theory and is reported as a descriptive constraint on undetected violating configurations.

Representative examples: Representative per-task shared responses and scoring traces (e.g., task-000001, task-000002, task-000003) show that the shared initial candidate matched the reference normalized configuration and that validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true for these examples; these representative artifact files and their recorded SHA-256 values are summarized in the artifact-verification paragraph below.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and what the run supports: Under the exact adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), validator set (two deterministic validators combined by logical OR), emulator, and the programmatic adversarial generator used here, initial LLM candidates satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for all sampled intents; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The archival artifacts consistently show model_calls_used = 300, per-episode validator traces with repair_applied = false, and the degenerate paired contingency (n11 = 300). This evidence supports the narrower claim that verifier insertion does not alter outcomes when baseline outputs already satisfy the chosen safety predicate under the chosen validator set and generation contract.

What the run does not show: Because no validator-detected violations occurred, the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate (target effect: 30 percentage-point absolute reduction); the observed degenerate contingency violates that assumption and renders McNemar inference uninformative for repair efficacy.

Design lessons (artifact-grounded): (1) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate saved model calls (300 vs up to 600) but substantially reduced independent-sample variance between arms; to exercise repair efficacy use independent-condition generation (two independent draws per pair) or increase pair/sample size. (2) Adversary potency matters: the programmatic adversarial perturbation used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability; stronger, targeted adversaries or red-team strategies are necessary to exercise repairs. (3) Verifier diversity and fidelity matter: using multiple oracle families, production-grade execution oracles, or emulators with richer device semantics will increase the chance of detecting realistic violations. (4) Reproducibility practicalities: per-episode raw responses, validator traces, provider-call audit, and the analysis log are archived and permit deterministic replay under the same contract.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation with declared model gpt-5-mini and two deterministic validators. The run completed N = 300 pairs with model_calls_used = 300 under shared_initial_candidate semantics and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate for all pairs (n11 = 300). Because no validator-detected violations occurred, no repair was invoked and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. The artifacts and analysis indicate that generation semantics, adversary design, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity materially determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable targeted follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, declared model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.

Model and verifier scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
